prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by reversible-terminator chemistry and clonal single-molecule readout

statement.case_for: Sequencing-by-synthesis is a chemical solution to a measurement problem: reversible terminators, engineered fluorophores and surface attachment chemistry let millions of strands be read in parallel. It changed what researchers and clinicians can actually do (population genomics, tumour profiling, prenatal screening, pathogen surveillance) and has been reproduced at enormous scale for two decades. Balasubramanian and Klenerman conceived and built the Solexa approach, which gives a defensible two-person core. After this round I still place it first, but by a narrower margin than in my opening.
statement.case_against: Credit is crowded: Rothberg's pyrosequencing-based platform, Mayer's colony sequencing and Ju's terminator chemistry are parallel contributions, and a two-person prize leaves them out. Some colleagues may also see sequencing as an enabling technology or as biology rather than chemistry. By contrast, B058 has broader support in the room (four top-three rankings) and arguably a cleaner chemical design principle, but its credit split is harder than B028's.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B028 first and would add Rothberg, because his 454 platform was the first commercial massively parallel system.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific merit, but I would not add Rothberg. His contribution is real, but the pyrosequencing route is chemically distinct and has been largely superseded, whereas the reversible-terminator route is the one that scaled and defined the field. A citation worded around reversible-terminator chemistry and clonal readout supports Balasubramanian and Klenerman without making them a compromise. I would still accept Rothberg if the committee judges that a prize on 'massively parallel sequencing' as a whole needs three names.

responses.point: Somfai ranks B021 (Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling) first as a mature, general method that changed how chemists build bonds, and treats Kosugi as a precursor.
responses.response: This is a strong case, and its attribution is cleaner than mine: Buchwald and Hartwig are an obvious pair. I disagree on ranking only because I give more weight to a discovery's reach beyond chemistry, and Pd-catalysed amination mostly changes how chemists work, within a field already honoured in 2010. I would not call it a weak candidate, though, and I think it belongs on the final ballot. On Kosugi I side with Somfai and Zou: the stoichiometric tin chemistry is a priority question that the citation can mention without adding a third laureate.

responses.point: Linke ranks the halide perovskite photovoltaic work (B003) first, noting its rapid efficiency gains and generative potential, but concedes that long-term stability is unresolved.
responses.response: I accept the physical-chemical case and the speed of progress, but I share your stability reservation, and in practice it matters more than for the other candidates. A material whose main application is not yet established as durable is harder to defend as having changed what people can do. The attribution is also very hard (Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel, Seok, Kanatzidis, at best three names). I rank it below B028 and B058 on maturity and credit.

responses.point: Sparr puts ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B058) second, framing them as a lipid self-assembly and phase-behaviour problem, with Cullis, Hope and Madden as the founding trio.
responses.response: I agree that B058 is chemistry and not just pharmacology, and the pKa-tuned ionizable lipid is the kind of molecular design principle I value. Your trio of Cullis, Hope and Madden, however, leaves out the lipidoid work of Anderson and Langer and MacLachlan's translation work, which three names cannot reconcile. That unresolved attribution, plus the 2023 Medicine prize for the mRNA side, is why I keep B058 as my first alternative and not my preferred pick. I am open to moving it up if the committee can agree a defensible allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards massively parallel sequencing as chemistry rather than biological technology.
Whether a three-person cap can fairly handle the Solexa, 454 and colony-sequencing contributions, and whether Rothberg should be included.
Whether the ionizable lipid nanoparticle credit (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson, Langer) can be allocated defensibly, given its broad support in the openings.
My account of the priority history among sequencing platforms rests on recollection, not verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. Linköping and my postdoc mentors (Stevens, Boey) are not credited on any shortlisted candidate. My research overlap with Emma Sparr (peptide-lipid self-assembly) is scientific, not personal, and bears most on B058 and B044.
